The resting metabolic rate of the Least gerbil (Gerbillus pusillus) has been quantified through respirometry trials conducted at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Under these standardized thermal conditions, the maximum basal oxygen consumption recorded was 13.48 milliliters per hour [JOi = 13.48 milliliters per hour], a value that reflects the elevated metabolic demands characteristic of small-bodied desert-dwelling murids at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Neonates of this diminutive species emerge from the birth canal after a relatively brief gestation, with newborn pups weighing just 1.8 grams [Wwb = 1.8 grams] at parturition. This low neonatal mass is typical of altricial rodents, where substantial energetic investment occurs postnatally through lactation. The modest birth weight stands in stark contrast to the ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, which reaches an average of 12.6 grams [Wwi = 12.6 grams], representing a more than sixfold increase in body mass from the neonatal stage to reproductive maturity. Such a pronounced growth trajectory underscores the species' rapid developmental pace, an adaptation to the ephemeral resource pulses and high predation pressure characteristic of its arid East African habitat.

Reproductive output in Gerbillus pusillus has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions mimicking the ambient thermal regime of its native range. At a stable ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], females typically produce litters containing 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4 pups per litter], a modest litter size consistent with the species' relatively small body size. The frequency of reproductive events is also constrained by the same thermal environment, with females giving birth to approximately 3 litters annually [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters annually], a rate that allows for multiple breeding attempts within a single favorable season. The gestation period supporting this remarkable reproductive schedule has been measured at 20 days [tg = 20 days] when females are maintained at 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], indicating that even minor fluctuations in ambient temperature can influence the pace of embryogenesis in this thermolabile rodent. The combination of a compact gestation window and a high annual reproductive rate allows the species to rapidly colonize temporary habitats following sporadic rainfall events.

The developmental chronology of the Least gerbil unfolds rapidly, a pattern consistent with its life-history strategy as a short-lived inhabitant of unpredictable environments. Maternal provisioning through lactation ceases remarkably early, with pups achieving nutritional independence and undergoing complete weaning at 20 days after birth [tx = 20 days after birth], a milestone that occurs at the same ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C] that governs many other life-history transitions. Following weaning, juvenile gerbils enter a period of accelerated somatic growth and physiological development, culminating in the attainment of sexual maturity. The estimated time since birth at puberty, based on comparative data from the congeneric species Gerbilliscus afra, is 93 days after birth [tp = 93 days after birth], again recorded at a thermal regime of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This rapid progression from birth to reproductive competence, achieved in just over three months, reflects a selective pressure to maximize the probability of breeding within a single short-lived seasonal window in the species' arid environment.

Longevity in Gerbillus pusillus is notably constrained, a life-history attribute that aligns with the species' elevated reproductive output and compact developmental timeline. The maximum lifespan documented in captivity, recorded under controlled conditions at an ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], reaches approximately 2008 days [am = approximately 2008 days], equivalent to roughly five and a half years. This relatively brief lifespan for a rodent of its size is consistent with the high extrinsic mortality rates characteristic of small desert mammals, where predation and environmental stochasticity impose a steep survival cost. Wild-living individuals are thought to have even shorter lifespans, with few individuals surviving beyond two or three reproductive seasons. The species' overall life-history syndrome—rapid maturation, large litters, high annual fecundity, and short lifespan—conforms to the classic r-selected strategy commonly observed in small-bodied murid rodents occupying unpredictable arid habitats.

The ecological context of the Least gerbil provides additional insight into its physiological and reproductive adaptations. Adult females, having achieved a maximum body mass of 12.6 grams [Wwi = 12.6 grams], are among the smallest members of the genus Gerbillus, a trait that limits their absolute energetic requirements but constrains their capacity to buffer against prolonged resource shortages. The resting metabolic rate of 13.48 milliliters per hour [JOi = 13.48 milliliters per hour] recorded at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] is comparatively high for a mammal of this mass, reflecting the elevated oxygen demand necessary to maintain homeothermy in the face of high thermal conductance across a small body surface area. In comparative terms, related species such as Gerbillus nanus exhibit similar metabolic scaling relationships, suggesting that the metabolic physiology of G. pusillus is broadly consistent with that of other small-bodied gerbils. The interplay between rapid reproduction, high metabolic demand, and abbreviated lifespan illustrates the finely tuned trade-offs that enable this species to persist in one of the world's most challenging terrestrial environments.
